title: React Native Fundamentals
summary: React's component model applied to real native primitives, how JavaScript reaches native code, and the two performance mistakes — blocking the JS thread and defeating memoization — that show up in almost every production app.

slides.markdown:
React Native takes React's component model — components, props, hooks, a virtual-DOM-style reconciliation step — and points it at real native views instead of HTML elements. The React part should feel immediately familiar to anyone who's used React on the web; what's genuinely different is everything downstream of `render()`: how a `<View>` becomes an actual `UIView`, and how JavaScript reaches platform APIs it doesn't natively have access to.

This topic covers the component model as applied here, the JS-thread/native-thread split (covered mechanically in [Cross-Platform Rendering Models](cross-platform-rendering-models)), native modules, engine choice, and Flexbox as the layout model — plus the two performance mistakes that show up in nearly every React Native codebase at some point.

The rules are identical to React on the web: components are functions (or classes) that take props and return a description of UI, state changes trigger re-renders, and a reconciliation algorithm diffs the new description against the old to compute a minimal set of changes. What's different is the vocabulary of what you're describing — ``, ``, ``, `` instead of `

Each of these maps to a real native view under the hood (`` becomes a `UIView`/Android `View`), not a simulated DOM element — this is the hybrid-native strategy from the rendering-models topic made concrete. The practical upshot: React developers' existing mental model — props flow down, state changes trigger re-renders, hooks manage local state and effects — transfers almost entirely, which is a large part of React Native's appeal for teams with existing React expertise.

slides.subTitle: calling platform APIs from JavaScript
slides.markdown:
React Native ships a large set of cross-platform components and APIs out of the box, but plenty of platform capability isn't covered — a specific biometric API, a hardware sensor, a brand-new OS feature. A **native module** is native code (Swift/Objective-C on iOS, Kotlin/Java on Android) that exposes a defined interface JavaScript can call, letting you reach anything the platform SDK exposes without waiting for the framework itself to add it.

Under the classic bridge, native module calls are async and serialize arguments/return values across the boundary; under the New Architecture, **TurboModules** use JSI to make these calls synchronous and lazily-loaded (a module only initializes on first use, improving startup time). Writing one is the standard escape hatch for 'the framework doesn't do this' — and a healthy React Native codebase typically has a handful, not zero, of these once it's past prototype stage.

| | Hermes | JavaScriptCore (JSC) |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | built by Meta specifically for React Native | Apple's general-purpose engine, also powers Safari |
| Startup time | faster — bytecode precompiled ahead of time | slower — parses and compiles JS at app launch |
| Memory footprint | lower, tuned for mobile constraints | higher, general-purpose |
| Default today | yes, on both iOS and Android in modern RN | legacy fallback |

Hermes precompiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time, so the app launches by loading and running bytecode directly rather than parsing and JIT-compiling raw JavaScript source on the device — this is the single biggest lever behind Hermes's faster cold-start numbers, and why it's now the default engine rather than an optional optimization.

The JS thread is a **single thread** — it handles component logic, event handlers, and (under the classic architecture) bridge traffic all in sequence. A heavy synchronous computation (parsing a huge JSON blob, a tight loop processing a large array) run directly in a render or event handler blocks that thread entirely, and everything waiting on it — including gesture responses and animations not otherwise offloaded to native — stalls until it finishes.

The fix depends on the work: genuinely CPU-heavy work can move to a separate JS context via a library like `react-native-worklets` or be offloaded to native code via a native module (doing the heavy lifting in Swift/Kotlin instead of JS entirely). For UI-thread-driven animations specifically, `react-native-reanimated`'s worklets can run the animation logic directly on the native/UI thread, sidestepping the JS thread for that specific interaction rather than trying to keep the JS thread merely 'fast enough.'

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: defeating memoization with a new prop every render
The senior nuance: know which layer a slowdown lives in
slides.markdown:
A junior answer treats 'React Native is slow' as one undifferentiated problem. A senior answer localizes it to a specific layer before touching code: is the JS thread saturated (check with the JS thread's own frame timing), is bridge/JSI traffic the bottleneck (check message frequency), or is the native side itself slow (a genuinely expensive native layout or an unoptimized image decode, which no amount of JS-side tuning fixes)?

The tooling matters here: Flipper (or its Perfetto-based successors) shows bridge traffic and native/JS timing side by side, and the React DevTools Profiler shows which components re-render and why on the JS side specifically. Naming the actual bottleneck layer, and the actual tool used to confirm it, is what separates 'I optimized it' from 'I have no idea what was actually slow and tried five things.'
